awards.question: When a river meets the sea, you can often see a visible line where freshwater meets saltwater. Why does this happen and why doesn't it just homogenise immediately?
awards.answer: Saltwater and freshwater don't mix easily due to different densities. You can see very clear boundaries, particularly with larger rivers like the Congo, Orinoco, Amazon. The warm water from the Mediterranean mixes by a process called 'salt fingering.' The phenomenon is called a 'salt wedge' - saline water comes up a river with fresh water going over the top due to density difference. This can kill fish that aren't adapted.

awards.question: Since the Christianization of Britain, why didn't the church change the names of the days of the week from their pagan origins (Tyr, Woden, Thor, Frigg, etc.)?
awards.answer: Alfred the Great DID try to Christianize the day names to move away from Germanic pagan gods (similar to Norse gods), partly to distinguish England from the Danes. However, it didn't take off - the common people weren't educated enough to change, and much of England was under Danish control at the time. The old names persisted. Saturday is named after Saturn (a Roman god) and nobody knows why. Sunday is Sunna's Day, day of the Sun. Sunna was actually a male sun god with a sister Mona (moon goddess), so they swapped the genders - we have feminine moon and masculine sun.

awards.question: How does a dog know which person to go to when two people with identical whistles from the same shop blow them at different ends of a field?
awards.answer: All dog whistles are manufactured to a very tight tolerance so they produce a consistent sound. When training your dog, you would typically train it to respond to specific commands - two pips for one command, three pips for recall. But inevitably, most dog trainers will tell you that your own personality comes into how you blow the whistle. Your dog will start to instinctively know it is YOUR whistle they are responding to. It's the relationship between the whistle and the blower. The only exception is the silent dog whistle with a screw piston - you can tune the frequency to your dog's ear if you wish.

Cosmetics also don't need to be labelled with hazard pictograms under CLP because they're already covered by their own specific regulations. awards.question: Why is one side of a bar of soap soft and the other side hard?
awards.answer: It's about the mould the soap is made in. The side that contacts the mould stays softer, while the side exposed to air cures faster and becomes harder. Not every soap does this - it depends on the mould type used.

awards.question: Why do we find beauty in inanimate objects? What is the evolutionary benefit?
awards.answer: We are genetically programmed to find environments most suitable for our species. It's called prospect and refuge. There's always an open space where we could find prey or plant food. We universally find flowers attractive because there's a location of future fruit. And there's always a little protected bit - refuge - hiding away from predators. There's always fresh water because our species needs that. This is hardwired into our DNA and the basis of every picturesque painting and garden design.

awards.question: When people were digging for coal or iron ore, how on earth did they know that what they were looking for was there?
awards.answer: There's something called the Order of the Strata put together by William Smith. He recognised that there was some sort of sequence - for example, if you find sandstone, then you might find limestone, and above that you might get mudstone, and then above that you might get coal. He recognised that too. The sequence of rocks repeats itself over time and you can fix these in time using the included fossils. So you know where you are in time and then you can figure out where you are in space. It's a great predictive tool. If you know the geology of a particular area, you can pretty much guarantee where you're going to find the coal. You go out and do some mapping and see where the rocks might be folded or where they're flat, follow these layers as they go up and down and cite your test drilling rigs accordingly.

awards.question: Does skin absorb water when swimming?
awards.answer: The outer layer of skin, the stratum corneum, is waterproof because it's made of dead flat cells called corneocytes in a mortar of lipids (cholesterol, ceramides). This layer is hydrophobic and prevents evaporation. Nicotine patches work because nicotine is oil soluble. Without this layer, you would dehydrate. The corneocytes can swell and absorb some water (causing wrinkles) but it won't go through the lipid layer.

awards.question: Where does all the rubber from car tyres go? It's not at the side of the road.

You get much more of it around junctions and traffic lights where people are braking - the energy of braking or cornering produces the tyre dust. awards.question: Will the Sahara run out of sand eventually? If so, how is it replaced? If not, how is it replenished?
awards.answer: No, it wouldn't run out because there's a relationship between the velocity of wind and atmospheric currents with the deposition of sand. The higher the velocity, the heavier the grains are able to be transported. When you see dust on your car window screen, it's always that finer material. The wind only transports the finer stuff and leaves behind the heavier stuff. So it would replenish. In the longer term, millions of years, if climate change made it more humid or maritime climate, you'd stop getting deposition of sand and get deposition of organic material and then the desert would disappear.

awards.question: What happens when there's a fire in a hospital if a surgeon is mid-operation? What if it's something that can't be stopped?

awards.question: How do deaf people learn to read? My three young boys have used phonics and sounds to learn to read, but deaf people can't hear the sounds being made out loud.
awards.answer: Deaf children learn to read through visual association, connecting signs or objects to printed words. If they have access to spoken language, they can make the connection between what they see and hear and the printed word. Many deaf children learn sign language - they learn the sign for an object (like 'ball'), understand the concept, then see the printed word and make the connection. For abstract concepts without physical representation, it works the same as hearing children - through conversation and language exposure. The more signs and language they have, the better their reading will be. Dr. Rowley is a deaf psycholinguist at the Deafness, Cognition, Language and Research Center.

awards.question: When you're diffusing a bomb, does it matter which wire you cut first?
awards.answer: The first thing you need to do is disconnect the power supply. IEDs work through an explosive chain - a small power supply creates a spark (like a short circuit or lighter flint), that initiates a slightly bigger explosion going into the detonation core, then finally the main charge. You establish where the power source is, then set up a remote device with a scalpel on the end using highly pressurised water, walk backwards, and fire it from a safe distance to cut through all the connections. The red, blue, green wires you see in films are mostly just for drama. The Oklahoma bomber was actually a former bomb disposal expert himself, which made his device very sophisticated.

awards.question: In cricket, why can't you be given out LBW if the ball pitches outside the leg stump, even if it's clearly going to hit the wicket? If it's going to smash the middle stump out of the ground but hits the pad just outside leg stump, the umpire gives it not out. Why?
awards.answer: The reason is to stop negative bowling. It's very difficult for a batsman to hit the ball when it's going down the leg side - they have to chase it around the corner. To stop bowlers from bowling negatively on the leg side and preventing scoring, they said you can bowl there if you like, but the batsman can just pad it away and cannot be out LBW. The historical reason is Bodyline in the 1930s when Harold Larwood bowled short-pitched stuff outside the leg stump and the Aussies could only play around the corner with fielders everywhere. It was considered ungentlemanly.

awards.question: When you pour a pint of beer, it gets a nice thick foamy head. But when you pour a pint of cola or lemonade, it doesn't. Why is that?
awards.answer: It's all about the gas used to push the drink from the barrel to the pump. Coke and soft drinks use 100% CO2. Guinness, Worthington, and cream flows use 70-30 gas (a mixture of nitrogen and CO2). Some lagers use 60-40. Nitrogen creates smaller, tighter bubbles that take longer to pop, giving a smoother, creamier mouthfeel and better head. CO2 gives a crisper, bubblier result. From a cask with an air compressor, there's not much head because no nitrogen is introduced.

awards.question: Why do kettles boil for 20 seconds too long?
awards.answer: Most kettles work via a steam tube - when water boils, steam builds up and travels down the tube to a bimetallic strip at the bottom, which switches the kettle off. If the kettle is half full, there's more water to heat before enough steam builds up to trigger the switch. This causes the delay. Electronic kettles without steam tubes don't have this problem.

awards.question: Why do we capitalise the letter I in English when no other languages do the same?

awards.question: Why the expression 'Philadelphia lawyer'? Why not Edinburgh, London, Chicago? Why specifically Philadelphia?
awards.answer: The Philadelphia lawyer refers to Andrew Hamilton, a lawyer from Philadelphia who defended John Peter Zenger in about 1740 in a landmark case. Zenger was a German immigrant publisher of the New York Journal who aired grievances against Governor William Cosby and was imprisoned. Hamilton's argument was that the jury could decide whether what was published was true, and if true, it could not be malicious. Zenger was acquitted, establishing truth as a defence of libel. The phrase's meaning changed over time - from about 1800 it meant competent and diligent, but in the second half of the 20th century it came to mean sleazy lawyer.

awards.answer: It goes back to the first days of cybernetics where scientists wanted to analyse closed systems. A closed system was called a black box and an open system was called a white box. It's a technical term, not a physical one. It describes a technological phenomenon, not a physical entity. It was also used to describe electronic boxes, but cybernetics made it more general. awards.question: Why are clouds different colours? You get dark grey rainy clouds, or big white fluffy ones where it never rains.
awards.answer: Clouds themselves don't glow - they only have colour from reflected light. Grey clouds are when there's not much light around, they're covering a lot of sky, very low down, or behind hills. In the evening when light goes through a lot of atmosphere and it's reddish, you get pink clouds. The orangey-green clouds last year were caused by fine dust from the Sahara reflecting light. When two clouds in the same sky are different colours, it's because they're picking up different lights - like a sunbeam through a hole making surrounding clouds brilliant white.

awards.question: Why does blood seep out of the bag when defrosting meat overnight, even though the bag is still sealed?
awards.answer: Two parts. First, the red liquid isn't actually blood - it's myoglobin, a protein in muscle tissue that looks like haemoglobin because it has iron in it. When cells freeze, they crack open and the myoglobin leaks out. Second, when you freeze meat in a plastic bag, the plastic freezes too and develops micro-tears that are big enough to let the myoglobin solution through - you'd need a microscope to see them but the plastic becomes porous.

awards.question: What's the origin of a judge's wig? Why do lawyers and judges wear wigs?
awards.answer: It's not a disguise - you'd wear a balaclava for disguise. It came from the Restoration when Charles II brought wigs over. Lawyers started wearing them after the rest of the population and never stopped. After the French Revolution, because of the powder tax, people stopped wearing powdered wigs, but barristers and judges continued.

awards.question: In life, in general, you can do most things left-handed. However, why can't you conduct an orchestra left-handed? I have friends who are Royal Marine musicians and they tell me you can't conduct an orchestra left-handed.
awards.answer: There are left-hand conductors out there, and it does drive the orchestra a bit potty. The way orchestral musicians train is: four beats in a bar - down for beat one, across to the left for beat two, back to the right for beat three, diagonally up for beat four. If you have a left-hand conductor, it's completely opposite to what they're used to. It's like driving on the other side of the road when you go on holiday - you can do it but it's hard and discombobulating.

awards.question: Why do some houses have a sparkling little metal thing on their chimneys that looks like an upside-down colander?
awards.answer: They're called revolving chimney cowls. They spin in the breeze and eradicate the downdraft - they draw the air up and out. So yes, they'll stop pigeons coming down, but that's not what they are - they're to stop that cold, biting wind that comes down Victorian chimneys into the fireplace.
